examples.problem_statement: Compute 11² using Vedic method for numbers above base 10.

solution.description: Compare 11 with the working base 10 and record how far above it sits: 11 is 1 more than 10, so the base is 10 and the excess is 1.

solution.operation: Apply Nikhilam Sutra: Add the excess to the number
solution.description: Because the number is above the base, add the excess back onto the number: 11 plus 1 gives 12. This 12 is the left-hand part of the answer.
Square the excess found in step 1: 1 times 1 is 1. This becomes the right-hand part, and under base 10 it occupies a single digit.
Place the left part 12 from step 2 in front of the right part 1 from step 3. Nothing needs carrying, so the digits read 121.
Check the shortcut against ordinary multiplication: 11 times 11 is 121, which matches the Vedic result.

examples.problem_statement: Compute 19² using Vedic method for numbers above base 10.

solution.description: 19 stands 9 above the base 10, so add that excess of 9 back onto 19. The sum 28 is the left-hand part.
Square the same excess: 9 times 9 is 81, which supplies the digits for the right-hand part.
Base 10 allows only one digit on the right, so keep the 1 of 81 and carry the 8 over to 28, making 36. Writing 36 in front of 1 gives 361.

examples.problem_statement: Compute 97² using algebraic explanation based on (a±b)² formula.

solution.description: 97 sits just under the round base 100, so rewrite it as 100 minus 3; the deficiency from the base is 3.
Expand with the identity for the square of a difference: 100 squared, minus twice 100 times 3, plus 3 squared, which is 10000 minus 600 plus 9.
Finish the arithmetic in order: 10000 minus 600 is 9400, and adding the 9 gives 9409.

key_reminders: {'point': 'For numbers above 10, instead of reducing by the deficit, increase the number by the surplus.'}
{'point': 'Extend the same rule to multi-digit numbers.'}
{'point': 'Use algebraic identities (a±b)² and a²−b² for justification.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: choose nearest power of 10 as base for easiest computation.'}

Subtracting the deviation instead of adding it. For 11 and 19, which sit above the base, the surplus is added to the number, not taken away.
Dropping the middle term when expanding 100 minus 3 squared, which turns 9409 into 10009.

solution.description: The most convenient working base for 59 is 50, and 59 sits 9 above it, so the deviation is plus 9.
Add the deviation to the number, 59 plus 9, to get 68. This is the left-hand part before the base adjustment.
Square the deviation: 9 times 9 is 81, which gives the right-hand part.
The working base is 50 rather than a plain power of ten, so scale the left part by it: 68 times 50 is 3400.
Add the right-hand part to the scaled left part: 3400 plus 81 is 3481, so 59 squared is 3481.
41 stands 1 above the working base 40, so the deviation is plus 1. The finished layout shown alongside is the left part 168 beside the right part 1.
The same deviation of 1 is entered on the second row as well, since squaring means multiplying 41 by itself and both rows carry the same excess.
Add the number to its deviation, 41 plus 1, giving 42 on the left, and square the deviation, 1 times 1, giving 1 on the right.
The working base 40 is 4 tens, so the left part must be multiplied by 4 to restore the true size of the answer.
That scaling turns 42 into 168 on the left, and with 1 on the right the answer reads 1681.
989 falls 11 short of the base 1000, so the deviation is minus 11. The completed layout is 978 on the left and 121 on the right.
The same deficiency of 11 belongs to the second row, because the number is being multiplied by itself.

Subtract the deficiency from the number, 989 minus 11, to get 978 on the left, and square the deficiency, 11 times 11, to get 121 on the right. Base 1000 leaves room for exactly three digits, so the answer reads 978121.
Choose a working base of 800 for 775: it is the round hundred taken 8 times, and 775 lies close to it.
775 falls 25 short of that working base, so the deficiency is 25. The finished layout is 6006 on the left and 25 on the right.
The same deficiency of 25 is written on the second row, as 775 is being multiplied by itself.
Subtract the deficiency from the number, 775 minus 25, to get 750 on the left, and square the deficiency, 25 times 25, to get 625 on the right.
The working base is 8 hundreds, so multiply the left part by 8: 750 times 8 is 6000.
The right-hand part may keep only the two digits 25 under a hundreds base, so the 6 of 625 carries into the left part: 6000 plus 6 is 6006, and the answer reads 600625.

solution.description: Take the part standing to the left of the final 5. For 15 that leading part is 1, and it is the previous number the sutra refers to.

solution.operation: Compute 'ekadhikena' — one more than the previous digit
solution.description: One more than the previous number: add 1 to 1, giving 2.

solution.operation: Multiply the previous digit by its ekadhikena
solution.description: Multiply the previous number by that successor: 1 times 2 is 2. This product forms the left-hand part of the square.

solution.operation: Append the square of the final digit 5
solution.description: The final digit 5 always contributes 5 times 5, that is 25, as the right-hand part, whatever the leading part happens to be.

solution.operation: Combine the two parts to get the final square
solution.description: Write the left part 2 in front of the right part 25 to read 225, so 15 squared is 225.

solution.description: Pick the power of ten nearest the numbers as the working base. Both 9 and 2 are handled against base 10.
Write each factor as the base minus its shortfall: 9 is 10 minus 1, and 2 is 10 minus 8.
Cross-subtract: take either number minus the other number's shortfall. 9 minus 8 is 1, and 2 minus 1 is also 1, which confirms the left-hand part is 1.
Multiply the two shortfalls keeping their signs: minus 1 times minus 8 is 8, the right-hand part.
Under base 10 the left part counts tens, so 1 times 10 plus 8 is 18, and 9 times 2 is 18.
The multiplier 99 is one short of 100, so reduce the other factor by one: 11 minus 1 is 10, the left-hand part of the product.

Subtract that left-hand part from 99 to get the right-hand part: 99 minus 10 is 89. In general a two-digit number times 99 reads as the number minus one, followed by 99 minus that reduced number, so 10 in front of 89 gives 1089.

key_reminders: {'point': 'We observe that the left-hand-side is invariably one less than the multiplicand and that the right-side-digit is merely the complement of the left-handside digit from 9.'}
{'point': 'And this tells us what to do to get both the portions of the product.'}
{'point': 'The word ‘Pūrṇa’ in this context has another technico-terminological usage and simply means the “multiplicand” (while the word ‘Apara’ signifies the multiplier).'}
{'point': 'The meaning of the sub-corollary thus fits in smoothly into its context i.'}

Subtracting the original 11 from 99 rather than the reduced left part 10, which gives 1088 instead of 1089.

The vertical step for the rightmost column multiplies the units digits. This gives the units digit of the final product.

The crosswise step multiplies the tens digit of the top number by the units digit of the bottom number, and adds the product of the units digit of the top and the tens digit of the bottom. This yields the tens digit of the final product (after handling any carry).
The vertical step for the leftmost column multiplies the tens digits. This gives the hundreds digit of the final product.
